entries.english:
Ancillary plaintiffs/applicants/interveners: Hans Ludwig, Valentin, and Martin von Lichtenstein zu Heilgersdorf (called Heiligsdorf in the file). Ancillary defendants/interveners: Bishop Julius of Würzburg; Andreas Lay, centgrave; and the judges and assessors of the prince-bishopric of Würzburg’s cent court at Seßlach. Plaintiffs’ attorney: Lic. Peter Paul Steurnagel (1615). Defendants’ attorney: Lic. Antonius Streitt (1593).

Contemporary description of the dispute: an order for distraint concerning money extorted from three imprisoned Christians and a Jew; also described as concerning money extorted from three imprisoned subjects of the Lichtensteins and the Jew Heyman.

The dispute concerned the jurisdiction of the cent court at Seßlach. In late April 1614, the court imposed on the community of Heilgersdorf its customary cent fine of 20 pounds per hearth after Heyman, the plaintiffs’ protected Jew who served as court reporter, failed to report that his windows had been smashed. When no payment was made, in early October 1614 the court imprisoned Heyman and the three plaintiffs’ subjects who had come to attend the court at Seßlach for four weeks to enforce its judgment (see order no. 8234).

Hans Ludwig, Valentin, and Martin von Lichtenstein saw this as an attempt to extend the cent court’s jurisdiction in Heilgersdorf. They said it was limited to serious criminal and capital cases—murder, arson, theft, and rape—and that the court was claiming authority over minor offenses subject to their own bailiff’s lordship and jurisdiction. The defendant bishop affirmed the reporter’s duty to report all offenses at the cent court. He stated that offenses committed in Heilgersdorf had also been reported there when the Seßlach office was pledged to the plaintiffs’ family (1536–1573). Reichskammergericht proceedings: 1616–1621 (recorded as 1616–1618).

The file contains: the 1168 privilege of Emperor Frederick I for Bishop Herold of Würzburg concerning jurisdiction in the Bishopric of Würzburg and the Duchy of Franconia; Emperor Charles V’s 1534 derogation privilege for Bishop Konrad II concerning prescription that had accrued during the Reformation; Charles V’s 1540 mandate against disobedient cent-court assessors in the bishopric, transcribed by the Reichskammergericht after all interested parties had been summoned in 1541, and Charles V’s 1545 confirmation, which incorporates King Charles IV’s 1347 privilege concerning the imperial provincial court of the Duchy of Franconia (Q 5–8; all printed); a compilation of minor and major criminal cases arising in Heilgersdorf and reported at the Seßlach cent court, 1536–1614 (Q 9); an extract from the Seßlach cent-court ordinance concerning suppression of reports (Q 10); the 1372 fief charter of Emperor Charles IV for Bishop Gerhard of Würzburg (Q 16); and Emperor Charles V’s 1532 exemption privilege for Bishop Konrad II concerning the Rottweil court of appeal (Q 17).

Extracts from the Würzburg Rotulus (see order no. 1565), Q 18: King Frederick III’s 1442 command to pay homage to Gotfried von Limpurg, administrator of the bishopric, authenticated in 1442 by Abbots Karl II of St. Burkard and Berthold of St. Stephan in Würzburg; a subsequent 1442 letter to the mayor and council of Würzburg from Wilhelm von Henneberg-Schleusingen, Georg von Henneberg-Aschach, (Wilhelm von) Castell, (Konrad von) Weinsberg, Herman von Schwarzenberg, Lorenz von Ostheim, Eucharius von Heßberg, Bernhard von Schaumberg, Siegmund von Thüngen, Adolf Marschall (von Ostheim), Caspar von Bibra, Karl von Bastheim, and Konrad von Klingenberg (nos. 6–7); extracts from agreements among Bishops Johann II, Johann III, Rudolf II, and Konrad II, the cathedral chapter, and the nobility of the Bishopric of Würzburg, dated 1412, 1456, 1467, and 1525, the last confirmed by Emperor Charles V in 1526 (nos. 8–11); the 1485 undertaking by Michael and Sigmund the Younger von Schwarzenberg, father and son, to hold Stephansberg Castle in fief solely from the bishopric, with the consent of Sigmund the Elder and Hans von Schwarzenberg, father and son (no. 12); and extracts from letters recognizing the bishopric’s territorial lordship: in 1485 by Berthold, Count and Elector of Mainz; Friedrich; Georg, Teutonic Order commander at Mergentheim; Heinrich, cathedral canon at Strasbourg; Otto von Henneberg-Aschach; and Margaretha, Countess of Henneberg-Schleusingen, née Duchess of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel; and in 1535 by Count Wolfgang of Hohenlohe (nos. 13–17).

Appendix volume to the Würzburg pleading of exceptions and proofs (see order no. 1565), Q 19: an extract from Bishop Johann III’s confirmation of the 1458 testament issued by Michael the Elder von Schwarzenberg after Abbot Mauritius III of the Würzburg Scottish monastery, acting as papal commissioner, had recognized his marriage to Ursula Frankengrüner; the 1477 judgment of the imperial provincial court of the Duchy of Franconia in Philipp von Weinsberg’s forfeiture suit against Reinhard Truchseß (von Baldersheim) concerning male fiefs at Unterbalbach, Reichelsburg (called Reigelberg in the file), and Burgerroth; an extract from the 1483 judgment of the imperial commissioners Elector Ernst and Duke Albrecht of Saxony in the dispute between Bishop Rudolf II of Würzburg and Count Friedrich von Henneberg-Aschach, together with the mayor, village headmen, and community of Linden, over an appeal from the imperial provincial court; an extract from the 1500 settlement between Bishop Rudolf II and Valentin von Bibra concerning redemption of the prince-bishopric’s share in Irmelshausen fortress, before the arbitrators Albrecht von Bibra, cathedral canon at Bamberg and Würzburg and provost of St. Johann zu Neumünster, and Bartholomäus von Herbilstadt; the 1489 acknowledgment by Christoph Fuchs (von Bimbach), prince-bishopric of Würzburg marshal and official at Zabelstein, that he had accepted Götz von Füllbach as a prince-bishopric servant and vassal; an extract from the 1489 order of Bishop Rudolf II and Count Otto von Henneberg-Aschach on proceedings against Hermann the Elder and Hermann the Younger Riedesel, father and son, after they had declared a feud against the count; and letters from Lorenz von Rosenberg to Bishop Melchior of Würzburg in 1550 and Hans Eucharius von Rosenberg to Bishop Julius in 1574 concerning complaints brought before the Reichskammergericht by Joachim von Niedeck and Zaisolph von Rosenberg respectively (see order no. 10946), together with the related 1551 judgment.

Also included is a schedule of cases involving nobles before the imperial provincial court of the Duchy of Franconia in 1499–1534, 1550–1554, 1560–1563, and 1570–1573 (Q 20).
